summary_grc: α ε η ι ο υ ω · αι ει οι αυ ευ ου · ἁ ἀ
summary_en: Seven vowels, long and short; the diphthongs; and the little marks that say whether a word starts with h.

grammar.md:
**Seven vowels.** α ε η ι ο υ ω. Two are always long: **η** (like the *e* in *there*, held) and **ω** (like *aw* in *saw*, held). Two are always short: **ε** (as in *pet*) and **ο** (as in *pot*). Three can be either: **α ι υ**. Length is a matter of time, not quality: a long *i* is simply a held *i*. **υ** is the French *u* / German *ü*: say *ee* with rounded lips.

**Diphthongs** are two vowels in one syllable: **αι** (*ai* as in *aisle*), **ει** (a long close *e*, *ay*), **οι** (*oi* as in *boil*), **υι**, **αυ** (*ow* as in *cow*), **ευ** (*e* + *u*, said quickly), **ου** (*oo* as in *food*).

**Breathings.** Every word that begins with a vowel carries a small hook over it. The **rough breathing** ἁ ἑ ἡ ἱ ὁ ὑ ὡ means the word starts with an *h*: ἵππος *hippos*, ὕδωρ *hudor*, ἥλιος *hēlios*. The **smooth breathing** ἀ ἐ ἠ ἰ ὀ ὐ ὠ means there is no *h*: ἄνθρωπος *anthrōpos*. Initial ρ always takes the rough one (ῥ, hence English *rh*ythm), and initial υ always has it too. On a diphthong the mark sits on the second letter: οἶκος, Εὐρώπη.

**Capitals** take the breathing beside them: Ἀθῆναι, Ἑρμῆς, Ἥρα.

culture.title: Writing on broken pots
culture.md: Athenians wrote on whatever was to hand: wax tablets, papyrus, lead, and above all **ostraka**, bits of broken pottery. The Agora excavations have turned up thousands of them, from shopping lists to the ballots of an *ostrakismos*, the vote by which the assembly could send a politician into ten years of exile. On many the breathings and accents you are learning are simply absent: they were invented by scholars in Alexandria two centuries after Ariston, to help readers who no longer spoke Attic natively. The spelling on the sherds, though, shows how the words really sounded.
